fetched_contents.text: Gradient boosting Machine learning technique Gradient boosting is a machine learning technique based on boosting in a functional space, where the target is pseudo-residuals instead of residuals as in traditional boosting. It gives a prediction model in the form of an ensemble of weak prediction models, i.e., models that make very few assumptions about the data, which are typically simple decision trees.[1][2] When a decision tree is the weak learner, the resulting algorithm is called gradient-boosted trees; it usually outperforms random forest.[1] As with other boosting methods, a gradient-boosted trees model is built in stages, but it generalizes the other methods by allowing optimization of an arbitrary differentiable loss function. History The idea of gradient boosting originated in the observation by Leo Breiman that boosting can be interpreted as an optimization algorithm on a suitable cost function.[3] Explicit regression gradient boosting algorithms were subsequently developed, by Jerome H. Friedman,[4][2] (in 1999 and later in 2001) simultaneously with the more general functional gradient boosting perspective of Llew Mason, Jonathan Baxter, Peter Bartlett and Marcus Frean.[5][6] The latter two papers introduced the view of boosting algorithms as iterative functional gradient descent algorithms. That is, algorithms that optimize a cost function over function space by iteratively choosing a function (weak hypothesis) that points in the negative gradient direction. This functional gradient view of boosting has led to the development of boosting algorithms in many areas of machine learning and statistics beyond regression and classification. Informal introduction (This section follows the exposition by Cheng Li.[7]) Like other boosting methods, gradient boosting combines weak "learners" into a single strong learner iteratively. fetched_contents.text: lightgbm - How leave's scores are calculated in this XGBoost trees? I agree with @user1808924. I think it's still worth to explain how XGBoost works under the hood though. * What is the meaning of leaves' scores ? First, the score you see in the leaves are not probability. They are the regression values. In Gradient Boosting Tree, there's only regression tree. To predict if a person like computer games or not, the model (XGboost) will treat it as a regression problem. The labels here become 1.0 for Yes and 0.0 for No. Then, XGboost puts regression trees in for training. The trees of course will return something like +2, +0.1, -1, which we get at the leaves. We sum up all the "raw scores" and then convert them to probabilities by applying sigmoid function. * How to calculate the score in leaves ? The leaf score (w) are calculated by this formula: w = - (sum(gi) / (sum(hi) + lambda)) where g and h are the first derivative (gradient) and the second derivative (hessian). For the sake of demonstration, let's pick the leaf which has -1 value of the first tree. Suppose our objective function is mean squared error (mse) and we choose the lambda = 0. With mse, we have g = (y_pred - y_true) and h=1. I just get rid of the constant 2, in fact, you can keep it and the result should stay the same. Another note: at t_th iteration, y_pred is the prediction we have after (t-1)th iteration (the best we've got until that time). Some assumptions: * The girl, grandpa, and grandma do NOT like computer games (y_true = 0 for each person). * The initial prediction is 1 for all the 3 people (i.e., we guess all people love games. Note that, I choose 1 on purpose to get the same result with the first tree. In fact, the initial prediction can be the mean (default for mean squared error), median (default for mean absolute error),... of all the observations' labels in the leaf). We calculate g and h for each individual: * g_girl = y_pred - y_true = 1 - 0 = 1. Similarly, we have g_grandpa = g_grandma = 1. * h_girl = h_grandpa = h_grandma = 1 Putting the g, h values into the formula above, we have: w = -( (g_girl + g_grandpa + g_grandma) / (h_girl + h_grandpa + h_grandma) ) = -1 Last note: In practice, the score in leaf which we see when plotting the tree is a bit different. It will be multiplied by the learning rate, i.e., w * learning_rate.

fetched_contents.text: 6 Gradient Boosted Decision Trees – Machine Learning for Economics In this chapter, we will combine our knowledge of decision trees and gradient decent optimization to learn about a very power machine learning framework: gradient boosted decision trees (GBDTs). At the time of writing GBDTs are the best performing models for medium sized tabular data, a position from which neural networks have not been able to displace them despite their great successes elsewhere. GBDTs belong to the class of ensemble models, models which pool together predictions from other models. The prediction from a GBDT is of the form \[f(x) = \sum_{i=0}^\infty f_i(x,\beta_i)\] where each \(f_i\) represents the prediction from a decision tree, with \(\beta_i\) is that tree’s parameters, representing in an abstract way its shape and splitting conditions. GBDTs are fit to data in a sequential way. We first fit a decision tree representing by \(f_0\), look at its errors, then fit \(f_1\) to best rectify those errors, and so on. This general approach is known as boosting and its development in the 1990s by Freund and Schapire, in the form of an algorithm called AdaBoost, was a major milestone in machine learning. We will see that the process of fitting GBDTs can be fruitfully viewed as gradient descent in a function space. But before we get into that, we need to review the loss function that we are aiming to minimize. Surrogate Loss Functions for Classification In this first section, we focus on surrogate loss functions commonly used in gradient boosting for classification. The true target in many classification tasks is a discrete label (e.g., \(y \in \{0, 1\}\) for binary classification). In the previous chapter on decision trees we looked at different performance measures such as accuracy for this task. However, with a discrete variable like \(y\) we cannot use the tools of differential calculus. To get around this we have our main model to output not the discrete class predictions but instead a score which reflects the model’s confidence that the observation belongs to a particular class. A very common score is the probability that the model assigns to an observation being in a certain class. We then define a proxy loss function, known as a surrogate loss function, that measures the ‘goodness’ of this score, and fit the model to minimize that. Once the model is fit, we can predict class membership if required on the basis of the scores. For example, if the scores are probabilities we might predict the observation to belong to that class which has the higest probability according to the model. The Exponential Loss The original AdaBoost algorithm, effectively used the exponential loss function. Suppose we have a dataset of \(n\) points \((x_i, y_i)\) where \(x_i\) is a feature vector and \(y_i \in \{-1, +1\}\) is a class label (for convenience, we sometimes let \(y_i \in \{-1, +1\}\) instead of \(\{0,1\}\) in this section). Our goal is to find a function \(F(x)\) that predicts a score. The final class label prediction being \(+1\) if the predicted score is positive, and \(-1\) if the predicted score is negative. The exponential loss is given by \[ L_{\mathrm{exp}}(y_i, F(x_i)) = \exp\bigl(-y_i \, F(x_i)\bigr). \] During training, if the model makes the correct prediction \(y_i\) and \(F(x_i)\) will have the same sign and hence \(y_iF(x_i)\) would be positive. On the other hand if the model makes an incorrect prediction \(y_i\) and \(F(x_i)\) would have opposite signs and \(y_iF(x_i)\) would be negative. Therefore, by calculating \(\exp(-y_i\,F(x_i))\) we get large losses for misclassification and small losses for correct classification. It turns out that the quantity \(y_iF(x_i)\), called the margin, is interesting not just for its sign. When the margin is a large positive number our model is not just correctly fitting the training sample, it is predicting the right answer with high confidence. When the margin is a large negative number it shows not only that the model is wrong, it is wrong with high confidence. It turns out fitting classification models to maximize the margin instead of just getting the right predictions on the training sample is a good way to get a model which also predicts well on new observations. In binary classification with labels \(y_i \in \{0, 1\}\) (or equivalently \(\{0, 1\}\) with some re-parameterization), we first derive the predicted probability that \(y_i = +1\) by the formula \[ p_i = \sigma\bigl(F(x_i)\bigr) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-F(x_i))}, \] and then define the loss to be the negative log-likelihood of the observed \(y_i\). \[ L_{\mathrm{log}}(y_i, F(x_i)) = -\Bigl[y_i \log p_i + (1-y_i)\log (1 - p_i)\Bigr], \] where \(p_i = \sigma(F(x_i))\). Log loss is more prevalent in modern machine learning frameworks due to its probabilistic interpretation. Minimizing log loss corresponds to maximizing the likelihood under a Bernoulli model. In practice, log loss has been found to be more robust than exponential loss. Accordingly, most gradient boosting libraries default to a variation of log loss for binary classification tasks. Gradient boosting determines the optimal leaf weight by combining the loss function’s gradients and Hessians, the tree splitting process that identifies the best split and leaf assignment, and the remaining residual or gradient in the leaf. The core idea is that each tree is built to correct the residuals from the previous model, and each leaf is assigned a value that optimizes the loss within that leaf [N1-F1][N1-R2][N3-F2].

First, the loss function and gradients determine the leaf contribution. In gradient boosting, the objective is to minimize an arbitrary differentiable loss function, and the algorithm uses gradient descent to move toward that minimum [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The gradient of the loss function, taken with a negative sign, gives the direction of steepest descent, while the Hessian provides curvature information that improves the update step [N4-R2][N4-F3]. In practice, for leaf weights, the gradient and Hessian are used to compute the optimal contribution of each leaf to the overall model [N3-F2]. For example, the leaf score is computed as the negative sum of gradients divided by the sum of Hessians plus a regularization term, which directly reflects how the loss changes with the leaf value [N3-F2]. This means the leaf contribution is not arbitrary but is tied to the local behavior of the loss function.

Second, the tree splitting process identifies the best split and leaf assignment. In gradient boosting, a tree is built iteratively: at each iteration, the algorithm fits a new weak learner to the residuals from the current model, and the tree is split to minimize the loss on the training data [N1-F1][N2-R2]. For a given node, the algorithm considers all possible splits and selects the one that leads to the largest reduction in the loss function. This process is repeated for each tree and each node, with the best split and leaf assignment determined by the loss decrease [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The splitting process is therefore a greedy optimization over the data, choosing splits that most improve the model’s ability to minimize the loss [N1-F1][N2-R2].

Third, the leaf weight is computed from the remaining residual or gradient in the leaf. After splitting, each leaf contains a subset of the data, and the leaf weight is determined by minimizing the loss for that subset. In the case of mean squared error, the leaf value is often the mean of the residuals in the leaf, while in more general settings, the leaf weight is derived analytically using the gradients and Hessians [N1-F1][N3-F2][N3-R4]. Specifically, the XGBoost formula for leaf scores shows that the leaf weight is a function of the summed gradients and Hessians, plus regularization parameters such as lambda [N3-F2]. This means the leaf weight is computed based on what remains in the leaf after splitting, not on the global dataset [N3-F2][N3-R4].

Overall, the optimal leaf weight is determined by the loss function’s gradient and Hessian, the splitting process that selects the best split and leaf assignment, and the residual or gradient remaining in the leaf [N1-F1][N2-R2][N3-F2].

## How the optimal leaf weight and corresponding objective function value are determined in gradient boosting trees

Gradient boosting determines the **optimal leaf weight** and the corresponding **objective function value** through a combination of three core ideas: minimizing the loss function using gradients and Hessians, splitting the tree to find the best split and leaf assignment, and computing leaf weights from the remaining residual or gradient in the leaf. The result is a local leaf value that improves the model fit while contributing to the global objective function [N1-F1][N2-R2][N3-F2].

---

## 1) What determines the optimal leaf weight

### The loss function and gradients determine the leaf contribution
In gradient boosting, the algorithm minimizes an arbitrary differentiable loss function by moving in the direction of steepest descent, where the gradient of the loss function indicates the direction of improvement and the Hessian provides curvature information [N1-F1][N4-F3]. This means the leaf contribution is not arbitrary: it is directly tied to the loss function’s derivatives.

In practice, the leaf weight is often computed using the gradients and Hessians of the loss function. For example, the leaf score in XGBoost is given by the formula $ w = -\frac{\sum g_i}{\sum h_i + \lambda} $, where $ g $ and $ h $ are the first and second derivatives of the loss, respectively, and $ \lambda $ is the L2 regularization term [N3-F2]. This formula shows that the leaf value depends on the local gradients and Hessians in the leaf, plus regularization.

### The tree splitting process identifies the best split and leaf assignment
Gradient boosting builds trees iteratively, fitting a new weak learner to the residuals from the current model [N1-F1][N2-R2]. At each node, the algorithm tries all possible splits and selects the one that maximizes the reduction in the objective function. Once a split is chosen, the data in each child node becomes a separate leaf, and the leaf assignment is determined by the best possible split at that node [N2-R2][N2-R4].

This means the leaf assignment is not computed independently from the split. Instead, the split and leaf assignment are determined together in a greedy way: the algorithm selects the split that gives the largest improvement in the loss, and then computes the leaf value for the resulting leaves [N2-R2][N3-F2].

### The leaf weight is computed from the remaining residual or gradient
After the tree is split, each leaf contains a subset of the data, and the leaf weight is determined by minimizing the loss for that subset. In the case of mean squared error, the leaf value is often the mean of the residuals in the leaf [N1-F1][N3-R4]. More generally, the leaf value is found by optimizing the loss function within the leaf, using gradients and Hessians, and regularizing the result with terms such as $ \lambda $ and $ \gamma $ [N3-F2][N3-R5].

So the leaf weight is computed from what remains in the leaf after splitting: the residual or gradient, plus any regularization constraints [N3-F2][N3-R4].

---

## 2) How the objective function is used to find the optimal leaf value

### What the objective function represents during tree construction
During tree construction, the objective function is the loss that gradient boosting seeks to minimize over the training data. The model is built as an additive sequence of weak learners, and each new tree is added to improve the model’s fit to the loss function [N1-F1][N2-R2]. In other words, the objective function is the quantity the algorithm is trying to reduce at every step.

### How the optimal leaf value minimizes the loss within a leaf
For a given leaf, the algorithm chooses the value that minimizes the loss for the data points in that leaf. In the simplest case, this is the mean of the residuals in the leaf, which minimizes squared error [N1-F1][N3-R4]. More generally, the leaf value is determined by solving an optimization problem that balances the loss reduction from the leaf against regularization terms such as L2 penalties and leaf penalties [N3-F2][N3-R5].

This means the leaf value is not chosen arbitrarily; it is the value that makes the loss as small as possible for the data in that leaf, subject to regularization constraints [N3-F2][N3-R5].

### How the tree chooses the best split and leaf values simultaneously
The tree chooses the best split and leaf values simultaneously because the splitting process and leaf value computation are tightly linked. At each node, the algorithm tries all possible splits and selects the one that gives the maximum reduction in the objective function. Once a split is chosen, the leaf values are computed based on the remaining residuals or gradients in each leaf [N1-F1][N2-R2][N3-F2].

This simultaneous selection means the split and leaf values are not computed in isolation. Instead, they are chosen together in a way that maximizes the improvement in the overall model fit [N2-R2][N3-F2]. The result is a tree that locally minimizes the loss while contributing to the global objective function [N1-F1][N2-R2].

---

## 3) Implementation-specific considerations

### How different implementations differ in leaf value computation
Across implementations such as XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost, the general principle is the same: leaf values are determined by gradients and Hessians, and regularization is applied to prevent overfitting [N5-F4][N2-R2][N4-F3]. However, the details can differ.

XGBoost explicitly uses the formula $ w = -\frac{\sum g_i}{\sum h_i + \lambda} $ for leaf scores, showing that leaf values are derived analytically from the loss function’s derivatives and regularization [N3-F2]. The evidence for LightGBM and CatBoost is thinner in this branch, but it indicates that the same principles apply in those implementations as well [N5-F4].

### Practical constraints such as minimum leaf size and regularization
Implementation-specific constraints also affect leaf value computation. Regularization terms such as $ \lambda $ and $ \gamma $ are used to penalize large or too many leaves, which helps prevent overfitting [N3-F2][N3-R5]. Minimum leaf size is a related practical constraint, though it is not explicitly described in the provided evidence for this node; in general, it is used to control the depth and granularity of the tree [N5-F4].

These constraints make the leaf value computation more stable and ensure the model does not overfit the data [N3-R5][N5-F4].

### How the final objective function value is aggregated across trees
Because gradient boosting is an additive model, the final objective function value is the cumulative result of all the trees’ contributions to minimizing the loss [N1-F1][N2-R2]. At each iteration, a new tree is added to improve the model’s fit, and the overall loss is reduced by the improvement from each tree [N1-F1][N2-R2].

## 4) How leaf-wise growth and regularization affect the optimal leaf value

### Leaf-wise growth changes the leaf value calculation
Leaf-wise growth changes the leaf value calculation by allowing the algorithm to expand the tree one leaf at a time, rather than one level at a time [N6-R2][N6-R5]. In this setting, the leaf value is often determined by the most promising residual or gradient in the current leaf, and the tree grows in a way that prioritizes the largest improvements.

LightGBM uses leaf-wise growth by default, and the evidence also notes that this strategy can be more efficient but may overfit more easily on smaller datasets [N6-R2][N6-R5]. This means leaf-wise growth can make the optimal leaf value more sensitive to the data and less stable than level-wise growth [N6-R4][N6-R5].

### Regularization terms influence the optimal leaf weight
Regularization terms such as $ \lambda $ and $ \gamma $ influence the optimal leaf weight by penalizing large or too many leaves [N3-F2][N3-R5]. This regularization means the optimal leaf weight is not just the value that minimizes the loss locally, but the value that also balances the loss reduction against the cost of adding more leaves.

In other words, regularization shrinks the leaf weight or suppresses the creation of new leaves when the benefit is small relative to the penalty [N3-F2][N3-R5]. This makes the leaf value computation more conservative and helps control overfitting [N3-R5].

### Shrinkage and learning rate affect the final model objective
Although shrinkage and learning rate are not explicitly defined in this node, the evidence implies that they affect the final model objective by controlling the magnitude of each tree’s contribution [N2-R2][N4-F3]. A smaller learning rate reduces the contribution of each tree, leading to a smoother, more gradual improvement in the objective function [N2-R2].

This also helps prevent overfitting by making the model learn more slowly and generalize better [N2-R2][N4-F3].

---
